sections.heading: Key points
sections.content:
*   Barking is normal canine communication, not a malfunction to be silenced. 
*   Dogs can't choose their environment, so humans should carry the larger burden of the conflict.
*   Suppressing barking with punishment silences the symptom, not the underlying need. 
*   Effective solutions start with the environment and teaching alternatives, not silence.

![Image 15: Robert Gramner/Unsplash](https://cdn2.psychologytoday.com/assets/styles/article_inline_half_caption/public/field_blog_entry_images/2026-09/robert-gramner-n6yqfpn_9n4-unsplash__1_.jpg?itok=K_OalIog)

Source: Robert Gramner/Unsplash

I recently wrote about what's wrong with ultrasonic bark deterrents, particularly when a neighbor aims one at someone else's dog. That piece raised a harder question: if we shouldn't punish a dog for barking, what should we do instead? The practical answer begins with figuring out why the dog is barking. But underneath that practical question is an ethical one, and I think it deserves more [attention](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/attention "Psychology Today looks at attention") than it usually gets.

Barking is not a canine malfunction. It's a normal, necessary form of canine communication—dogs bark to alert, warn, greet, protest, express excitement, seek attention, or respond to something that has caught their notice. When barking becomes "a problem," we're really asking a dog to modify a fundamental part of being a dog because of the conditions of human life. And those conditions can be genuinely difficult: enormous numbers of dogs now live in apartments and dense neighborhoods, often just feet from human neighbors, with little room to move, vocalize, or simply be a dog without affecting someone else.

This is a structural problem. And even though nuisance barking often gets framed as a dog-human conflict, more often it's a human-human conflict in which the dog is caught in the middle: The neighbor wants to sleep, the dog wants to bark, and the guardian has responsibilities to both. The ethical question, then, isn't how to quiet the dog. It's how to negotiate competing human interests while minimizing the burden placed on the dog who didn't create any of them.

sections.heading: Not all barking is the same problem
sections.content:
As I noted above, the first practical step is figuring out what kind of barking is actually happening. As trainer Pat Miller has emphasized, identifying the function of the barking should come before choosing a response to it, and Patricia McConnell makes a similar point: a bark might mean anything from _put my dinner bowl down_ to _there's a monster in the driveway_. That distinction matters ethically, because the same intervention can have very different consequences depending on what's driving it. A dog barking from terror is not having the same experience as one barking because she wants to play, and a device that simply silences barking doesn't distinguish between them; it treats the vocalization itself as the problem, when often the barking is the dog telling us what the problem actually is.

That's the trouble with treating barking like a bad habit to be extinguished: It puts the entire burden on the dog, who has almost no control over the circumstances she lives in. Humans choose the apartment, the schedule, the hours of solitude, the proximity of other people—and then ask the dog to adapt to all of it. Dogs can and should learn to navigate difficult environments, but there's an important difference between helping a dog learn to cope and punishing her for a perfectly normal behavior. A shock, spray, or ultrasonic device may reduce the barking, but silence by itself tells us nothing about whether the dog's underlying needs have been addressed. A frightened dog can become quieter without becoming less frightened. Suppressing something dogs evolved to do, without resolving what's driving it, strikes me as ethically backward.

sections.heading: Taking responsibility without shifting the cost
sections.content:
None of this means neighbors should have to tolerate constant disruption. If your dog is disturbing the people around you, it's your responsibility as her guardian to do something about it—"dogs bark, get over it" isn't a good enough answer, and your neighbors shouldn't have to surrender their sleep or quiet work space because of a choice you made. But taking responsibility doesn't mean making the dog absorb the entire cost. It means looking for solutions that distribute the burden more fairly, starting with [the environment](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/environment "Psychology Today looks at the environment") rather than the dog herself. If she spends the afternoon barking at passersby, close the blinds or move her away from the window. If fence-line barking is the issue, don't leave her outside for hours rehearsing it. Exercise, enrichment, and rest matter too; [management](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/leadership "Psychology Today looks at management") isn't giving in to the dog but changing the circumstances so she isn't spending her day responding to an environment that's asking too much of her.

From there, training can teach a dog what to do _after_ she notices something, rather than teaching her the world is invisible. She's allowed to notice a stranger or hear a noise, and we can help her learn what to do next. McConnell describes an "Enough" cue that means, essentially, move away and come to me, so the sequence becomes: notice, alert, orient toward the guardian, settle. That's a very different message than [punishment](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/punishment "Psychology Today looks at punishment") sends. One teaches the dog how to handle the situation; the other just makes the original behavior costly.

The same logic applies to [fear](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/fear "Psychology Today looks at fear")-based barking, which needs distance and gradual counterconditioning rather than suppression, and to barking that functions as a request—for attention, for the door, for a ball—which can often be redirected toward another behavior without eliminating the dog's ability to communicate at all. Teaching a dog to settle, to tolerate stillness without treating every sound as an emergency, helps too. But it's worth holding onto the distinction: Calmness can be learned, while silence can be imposed, and those are not the same achievement.

sections.heading: The conflict belongs to us
sections.content:
Ultimately, this is bigger than dog training. We've built environments in which huge numbers of dogs live in close proximity to people with limited tolerance for canine behavior, and clever training won't make every version of that conflict disappear. What we can do is acknowledge the structural problem and ask who has the power to absorb its costs. The dog has the least. She didn't choose the apartment, the neighborhood, or the three feet separating her yard from someone else's bedroom window. Humans made those arrangements, and so dogs live within social expectations they had no part in setting.

The human guardian should carry the larger share of the work in resolving the conflict—closing blinds, adjusting routines, hiring help, consulting a behavior professional, or simply having an honest conversation with a neighbor about what's being done and when it's hardest for them. That conversation recognizes something worth holding onto: The neighbor isn't the enemy, and neither is the dog. The humans are the ones trying to figure out how to share a world. Once we see it that way, the real question isn't _how do I make my dog stop barking_, but _how do I resolve this without making her pay for a problem humans created_.

### Key points

*   Barking is normal canine communication, not a malfunction to be silenced. 
*   Dogs can't choose their environment, so humans should carry the larger burden of the conflict.
*   Suppressing barking with punishment silences the symptom, not the underlying need. 
*   Effective solutions start with the environment and teaching alternatives, not silence.

I recently wrote about what's wrong with ultrasonic bark deterrents, particularly when a neighbor aims one at someone else's dog. That piece raised a harder question: if we shouldn't punish a dog for barking, what should we do instead? The practical answer begins with figuring out why the dog is barking. But underneath that practical question is an ethical one, and I think it deserves more [attention](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/attention "Psychology Today looks at attention") than it usually gets.

Barking is not a canine malfunction. It's a normal, necessary form of canine communication—dogs bark to alert, warn, greet, protest, express excitement, seek attention, or respond to something that has caught their notice. When barking becomes "a problem," we're really asking a dog to modify a fundamental part of being a dog because of the conditions of human life. And those conditions can be genuinely difficult: enormous numbers of dogs now live in apartments and dense neighborhoods, often just feet from human neighbors, with little room to move, vocalize, or simply be a dog without affecting someone else.

This is a structural problem. And even though nuisance barking often gets framed as a dog-human conflict, more often it's a human-human conflict in which the dog is caught in the middle: The neighbor wants to sleep, the dog wants to bark, and the guardian has responsibilities to both. The ethical question, then, isn't how to quiet the dog. It's how to negotiate competing human interests while minimizing the burden placed on the dog who didn't create any of them.

## Not all barking is the same problem

As I noted above, the first practical step is figuring out what kind of barking is actually happening. As trainer Pat Miller has emphasized, identifying the function of the barking should come before choosing a response to it, and Patricia McConnell makes a similar point: a bark might mean anything from _put my dinner bowl down_ to _there's a monster in the driveway_. That distinction matters ethically, because the same intervention can have very different consequences depending on what's driving it. A dog barking from terror is not having the same experience as one barking because she wants to play, and a device that simply silences barking doesn't distinguish between them; it treats the vocalization itself as the problem, when often the barking is the dog telling us what the problem actually is.

That's the trouble with treating barking like a bad habit to be extinguished: It puts the entire burden on the dog, who has almost no control over the circumstances she lives in. Humans choose the apartment, the schedule, the hours of solitude, the proximity of other people—and then ask the dog to adapt to all of it. Dogs can and should learn to navigate difficult environments, but there's an important difference between helping a dog learn to cope and punishing her for a perfectly normal behavior. A shock, spray, or ultrasonic device may reduce the barking, but silence by itself tells us nothing about whether the dog's underlying needs have been addressed. A frightened dog can become quieter without becoming less frightened. Suppressing something dogs evolved to do, without resolving what's driving it, strikes me as ethically backward.

## Taking responsibility without shifting the cost

None of this means neighbors should have to tolerate constant disruption. If your dog is disturbing the people around you, it's your responsibility as her guardian to do something about it—"dogs bark, get over it" isn't a good enough answer, and your neighbors shouldn't have to surrender their sleep or quiet work space because of a choice you made. But taking responsibility doesn't mean making the dog absorb the entire cost. It means looking for solutions that distribute the burden more fairly, starting with [the environment](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/environment "Psychology Today looks at the environment") rather than the dog herself. If she spends the afternoon barking at passersby, close the blinds or move her away from the window. If fence-line barking is the issue, don't leave her outside for hours rehearsing it. Exercise, enrichment, and rest matter too; [management](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/leadership "Psychology Today looks at management") isn't giving in to the dog but changing the circumstances so she isn't spending her day responding to an environment that's asking too much of her.

From there, training can teach a dog what to do _after_ she notices something, rather than teaching her the world is invisible. She's allowed to notice a stranger or hear a noise, and we can help her learn what to do next. McConnell describes an "Enough" cue that means, essentially, move away and come to me, so the sequence becomes: notice, alert, orient toward the guardian, settle. That's a very different message than [punishment](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/punishment "Psychology Today looks at punishment") sends. One teaches the dog how to handle the situation; the other just makes the original behavior costly.

The same logic applies to [fear](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/fear "Psychology Today looks at fear")-based barking, which needs distance and gradual counterconditioning rather than suppression, and to barking that functions as a request—for attention, for the door, for a ball—which can often be redirected toward another behavior without eliminating the dog's ability to communicate at all. Teaching a dog to settle, to tolerate stillness without treating every sound as an emergency, helps too. But it's worth holding onto the distinction: Calmness can be learned, while silence can be imposed, and those are not the same achievement.

## The conflict belongs to us

Ultimately, this is bigger than dog training. We've built environments in which huge numbers of dogs live in close proximity to people with limited tolerance for canine behavior, and clever training won't make every version of that conflict disappear. What we can do is acknowledge the structural problem and ask who has the power to absorb its costs. The dog has the least. She didn't choose the apartment, the neighborhood, or the three feet separating her yard from someone else's bedroom window. Humans made those arrangements, and so dogs live within social expectations they had no part in setting.

That conversation recognizes something worth holding onto: The neighbor isn't the enemy, and neither is the dog. The humans are the ones trying to figure out how to share a world. Once we see it that way, the real question isn't _how do I make my dog stop barking_, but _how do I resolve this without making her pay for a problem humans created_.
